rawInput.complaint: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with a history of total abdominal hysterectomy 20 years earlier for fibroids presented with a 1-year history of clitoral enlargement, hirsutism, deepening of voice, decreased libido, and increasing abdominal girth. Baseline renal and hepatic chemistries, TSH, and lipid panel were unchanged from 1 year prior except for mildly elevated LDL. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an anechoic, nonvascular, cystic left adnexal lesion measuring 10.5 × 5.9 × 6.2 cm. CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed the cystic left adnexal mass and demonstrated no adrenal mass or other intra-abdominal abnormalities. Initial hyperandrogenism workup revealed a free testosterone of 4.2 pg/ml (normal) but a total testosterone of 264.3 ng/dl (elevated), with DHEA-S 29.2 μg/dl, CA-125 5 U/ml, and inhibin-A 1 pg/ml all within normal limits. Three months later, the cyst was unchanged but symptoms persisted. On referral to endocrinology, repeat labs showed free testosterone 4.7 pg/ml, total testosterone 276 ng/dl, FSH 41.7 IU/L, LH 26.6 IU/L (postmenopausal range), suppressed 8 am cortisol of 1.0 μg/dl, and normal DHEA, DHEA-S, and estradiol. Repeat ultrasound showed slight increase of the adnexal mass to 11.7 × 5.5 × 8.3 cm. A multidisciplinary team recommended laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief concern is progressive virilization in a 60-year-old postmenopausal woman: clitoral enlargement, hirsutism, deepening of voice, decreased libido, and increasing abdominal girth over 1 year. In a postmenopausal patient, new virilization is concerning for an androgen-secreting neoplasm until proven otherwise.

Salient positive findings strongly support an ovarian source of androgen excess. Total testosterone is markedly elevated on two occasions (264.3 and 276 ng/dl), while DHEA and DHEA-S are normal, which argues against an adrenal androgen source. CT showed no adrenal mass or other intra-abdominal abnormality. Imaging repeatedly demonstrated a persistent enlarging left adnexal cystic lesion, from 10.5 cm to 11.7 cm, temporally matching the symptoms. Gonadotropins (FSH 41.7, LH 26.6) are in the postmenopausal range, so this is not explained by a premenopausal functional state. Estradiol is normal, CA-125 is low, and inhibin-A is normal, which makes common estrogenic sex-cord stromal tumors less likely but does not exclude an androgen-producing ovarian tumor. The patient also has prior hysterectomy, so uterine bleeding clues are unavailable.

Pertinent negatives help narrow the differential. There is no adrenal mass on CT, and DHEA/DHEA-S are normal, making adrenal adenoma/carcinoma less likely. There is no mention of exogenous androgen use. The degree of virilization and testosterone elevation are not typical for common postmenopausal PCOS-type physiology. The lesion is described as anechoic, nonvascular, and cystic rather than a classic solid ovarian stromal mass, but persistent enlargement plus biochemical hyperandrogenism still supports an ovarian process. Normal inhibin-A makes granulosa/thecoma-spectrum tumors less likely, though not impossible. Suppressed morning cortisol is noted, but with no adrenal mass and no clinical syndrome provided, it does not better explain the virilization.

Candidate differentials considered:
1. Androgen-secreting ovarian tumor fits best because of rapid virilization after menopause, total testosterone well above normal, normal adrenal androgens, no adrenal mass, and a persistent enlarging adnexal mass. Among ovarian tumors, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor is a classic virilizing tumor, but these are usually solid and occur in younger women. Steroid cell tumor is another strong consideration because it often presents in peri/postmenopausal women with marked androgen excess and virilization.
2. Ovarian hyperthecosis can cause postmenopausal hyperandrogenism and virilization with elevated testosterone and normal/low DHEA-S. However, it more often causes bilateral ovarian stromal enlargement rather than a single large unilateral cystic adnexal mass.
3. Adrenal androgen-secreting tumor is less likely because DHEA/DHEA-S are normal and CT showed no adrenal lesion.
4. PCOS is low likelihood given the patient is postmenopausal with new-onset virilization and markedly elevated testosterone; PCOS usually begins earlier and rarely causes this degree of virilization.

Narrowing to one diagnosis: the combination of postmenopausal virilization, repeatedly elevated total testosterone, normal DHEA/DHEA-S, absent adrenal lesion, and a persistent enlarging unilateral adnexal mass makes an androgen-secreting ovarian neoplasm the single best diagnosis. Given the age group and biochemical pattern, the most likely specific diagnosis is an ovarian steroid cell tumor.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Ovarian steroid cell tumor (androgen-secreting ovarian tumor)
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Progressive virilization after menopause, total testosterone 264-276 ng/dl, normal DHEA/DHEA-S, no adrenal mass on CT, and persistent enlarging unilateral adnexal mass.

Postmenopausal hyperandrogenism with elevated testosterone and normal adrenal androgens can occur, but this usually causes bilateral ovarian stromal enlargement rather than a large unilateral cystic lesion.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor of the ovary
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Classic virilizing ovarian tumor causing elevated testosterone, but typically occurs in younger women and is more often solid than a large simple cystic mass.
Would more often raise DHEA/DHEA-S and/or show an adrenal mass; both adrenal labs and CT are not supportive.
New-onset virilization in a 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with markedly elevated testosterone is atypical for PCOS.
